organism: Human papillomavirus, a family of small double-stranded DNA viruses that infect epithelium; more than 200 distinct types have been identified. Most types infect cutaneous epithelium and cause common skin warts. About 40 types infect mucosal epithelium and are categorized by their association with cervical cancer: low-risk/nononcogenic types (e.g. 6, 11) cause anogenital warts and low-grade cell abnormalities, while high-risk/oncogenic types (including 16 and 18) act as carcinogens - high-risk HPV is detected in 99% of cervical precancers, and type 16 alone causes about half of cervical cancers worldwide.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Most HPV infections are asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously within a year or two; only a small proportion become persistent, but persistent infection is the key risk factor for progression to cancer. Clinical manifestations include anogenital warts, recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (rarely, via vertical transmission from an infected mother), cervical cancer precursor lesions (detected through screening as squamous intraepithelial lesions, formerly called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia), and cancers of the cervix, anus, vagina, vulva, penis, and oropharynx. Infection with one HPV type does not prevent infection with another - 5%-30% of people infected with a mucosal type carry multiple types.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only natural reservoir; other papillomaviruses infect other species. Transmission is through intimate skin-to-skin contact, most often during vaginal, penile, anal, or oral sex, and infection typically occurs soon after first sexual activity (40% cumulative incidence by 24 months post-first-intercourse in one cohort study of college women). There is no seasonal pattern, and communicability is presumed high given the very large number of new infections each year. Risk is primarily tied to sexual behavior, especially higher numbers of lifetime and recent sex partners.
secularTrendsSummary: Genital HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the US and worldwide; an estimated 79 million people were infected and about 14 million new infections occurred annually in the prevaccine era (2003-2006 data), nearly half in people 15-24. HPV causes an average of 43,999 cancers annually in the US (24,886 in women, 19,113 in men) - including about 91% of cervical cancers, 91% of anal cancers, 70% of oropharyngeal cancers, and smaller majorities of vulvar, vaginal, and penile cancers. Within a decade of the 2006 US vaccine introduction, prevalence of vaccine-targeted types (6, 11, 16, 18) fell 86% among females 14-19 and 71% among females 20-24; anogenital wart prevalence and high-grade cervical lesion rates have both fallen in the vaccine era. Among adolescents 13-17 in 2019, 71.5% had received at least 1 dose and 54.2% were up to date.
vaccineDescription: The vaccine antigen is HPV's L1 major capsid protein, produced by recombinant DNA technology in yeast; L1 proteins self-assemble into noninfectious, nononcogenic virus-like particles (VLPs). A quadrivalent vaccine (4vHPV, Gardasil, types 6/11/16/18) was licensed in 2006 and a bivalent vaccine (2vHPV, Cervarix, types 16/18) in 2009; both remain licensed but are no longer distributed in the US. The 9-valent vaccine (9vHPV, Gardasil 9, types 6/11/16/18/31/33/45/52/58) was licensed in 2014 and is the only product currently distributed. All are given intramuscularly; 9vHPV contains yeast protein and aluminum adjuvant, no antibiotic or preservative.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine vaccination is recommended at age 11-12 (series can start as early as age 9); catch-up vaccination is recommended for everyone through age 26 who isn't adequately vaccinated. The number of doses depends on age at the first valid dose: a 2-dose series (0, 6-12 months, minimum interval 5 months) for immunocompetent people who start before their 15th birthday; a 3-dose series (0, 1-2, 6 months) for anyone starting on or after their 15th birthday, or with an immunocompromising condition regardless of age. There is no maximum interval between doses, and an interrupted series does not need to restart. HPV vaccines are not licensed for use past age 45.
vaccineEfficacySummary: HPV vaccine is highly immunogenic - more than 98% of recipients develop an antibody response to each covered type within a month of completing the series, though no minimum protective antibody titer has been established (efficacy has been too high in trials to identify a threshold). Ongoing monitoring shows vaccine effectiveness above 90% with no waning through at least 10-12 years. Efficacy is high in people not yet exposed to a given vaccine-covered type at vaccination, but the vaccine has no therapeutic effect on infection or disease already present at vaccination - it is purely prophylactic. Prior infection with one vaccine-covered type does not reduce efficacy against the other covered types.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is a history of immediate hypersensitivity to yeast (4vHPV and 9vHPV, both yeast-produced) or an anaphylactic allergy to latex (2vHPV only, whose prefilled syringe tip cap may contain latex). Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. HPV vaccines are not recommended during pregnancy - if pregnancy is discovered mid-series, the remaining doses should wait until after delivery, though a dose inadvertently given during pregnancy requires no intervention and pregnancy testing is not needed beforehand. Lactating/breastfeeding people can receive the vaccine.
vaccineSafetySummary: HPV vaccine is generally well tolerated. Local reactions (pain, redness, swelling) are the most common adverse events, reported by 20%-90% of prelicensure trial recipients and increasing somewhat with each successive dose; a temperature of 100F was reported by 10%-13% of recipients, similar to placebo recipients. Anaphylaxis is rare but can occur. Postlicensure VAERS and Vaccine Safety Datalink monitoring (including around 839,000 9vHPV doses in 2015-2017) has not identified any new or unexpected safety signal. Because syncope has occasionally been reported after HPV vaccination, recipients should be seated during administration and observed for about 15 minutes afterward.
vaccineStorageSummary: HPV vaccines must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: HPV infection is NOT a nationally notifiable condition in the US. Cancer burden attributable to HPV is instead tracked through the National Cancer Institute's SEER program and CDC's National Program of Cancer Registries. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for general reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Shared Clinical Decision-Making for Adults 27-45
supplementalTopics.summary: Catch-up vaccination is not routinely recommended for anyone over 26, since population-level benefit at that age is minimal - most sexually active adults have already been exposed to some vaccine-covered types, and there's no clinical test to determine which types a given person remains susceptible to. Instead, ACIP recommends individualized shared decision-making for adults 27-45 who aren't adequately vaccinated, weighing factors like a new sex partner (a risk factor for new infection at any age), a long-term mutually monogamous relationship (low new-infection risk), and the fact that vaccine effectiveness may be lower in someone with multiple lifetime partners and likely prior exposure to covered types.

supplementalTopics.title: Cervical Cancer Screening Still Required
supplementalTopics.summary: HPV vaccination does NOT eliminate the need for continued cervical cancer screening, since up to 30% of cervical cancers are caused by types the quadrivalent/bivalent vaccines don't cover, and 15% by types even the 9-valent vaccine doesn't cover. Vaccinated people should be screened the same as unvaccinated people: cytology every 3 years from age 21-29, then (age 30-65) a choice of cytology every 3 years, HPV testing alone every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. Annual screening is not recommended for average-risk individuals, and screening is not recommended before age 21.

keyPoints: The link between cervical cancer and sexual behavior was suspected for over a century before HPV DNA was found in cervical cancer cells in the early 1980s
9 out of 10 cervical cancers, and about 7 in 10 oropharyngeal cancers, are attributable to HPV
The number of doses needed depends entirely on age at the first dose: 2 doses if started before age 15, 3 doses if started at 15 or older (or if immunocompromised at any age)
The vaccine is purely prophylactic - it has no therapeutic effect on an HPV infection or disease already present at the time of vaccination
No prevaccination testing (HPV testing, Pap testing, pregnancy testing) is needed or recommended before vaccinating
Vaccinated people still need routine cervical cancer screening, since current vaccines don't cover every cancer-causing HPV type
HPV infection is not a nationally notifiable condition - burden is tracked through cancer registries instead
